title: How Area Codes Work: NPA-NXX-XXXX Explained
desc: What the three parts of a North American phone number mean, how area and exchange codes are built, and why 0 and 1 are special digits.
h1: How North American area codes work
lede: A North American telephone number is three codes stacked together: an area code, an exchange code and a four-digit line number.
body:
Three parts, ten digits

Every number in the North American Numbering Plan (NANP) follows the same pattern: NPA-NXX-XXXX. The first three digits are the Numbering Plan Area, or area code. The next three are the NXX, the central office code, sometimes called the exchange code. The last four are the line number, assigned by whichever carrier serves that exchange. An example makes the split obvious: in 212-555-0142, the area code is 212, the exchange is 555 and the subscriber line is 0142.

What the area code identifies

An area code identifies a numbering plan area: a region, usually covering many towns and telephone exchanges, drawn so that a place can grow without exhausting its numbers. Area codes are not city boundaries. One code can cover a whole province or a large slice of a state, and a large city can carry several codes at once because it is split across several exchanges. The code is really a routing label: network equipment uses it to send a call toward the right part of the system, and the digits after it narrow the destination down to one line.

Why 0 and 1 are excluded from the leading position

No area code and no exchange code begins with 0 or 1. Those digits are reserved in the North American plan: 0 reaches an operator, and 1 is the trunk prefix that tells the network a long-distance number follows. That is why the first digit of every NPA and every NXX is 2 through 9, and why 012-555-0142 cannot be a valid number. The rule is structural, not cosmetic: it lets a switch tell a dialed area code apart from an operator or trunk signal.

The exchange code (NXX)

The NXX pins a number to one central office, a switching centre that serves a defined area, often a single town or a neighbourhood in a city. Its first digit is again 2 through 9. Combinations of the N11 shape are excluded: 211, 311, 411, 511, 611, 711, 811 and 911 are held aside for short-code services, which is why 911 can never be an area code or an exchange code.

The middle digit, then and now

In the plan's original design every geographic area code was written N 0/1 X, so the middle digit had to be 0 or 1. That capped the system at 160 geographic codes (8 x 2 x 10), which was generous when the plan was drawn up but far too small later. When those combinations ran out, the restriction was dropped and codes with any middle digit were assigned. That history explains the split people notice today: older codes such as 201, 310, 415 and 519 have 0 or 1 in the middle, while newer ones such as 234, 332 and 458 do not. The middle digit carries no routing meaning now; it is simply part of the three-digit code.

The line number

The last four digits are the part most people never think about. Within one exchange code there are 10,000 possible line numbers, from 0000 through 9999, and the carrier allocates them as service is ordered. Change the last four digits and you have a different customer on the same switch.
faq: Can an area code start with 0 or 1?
No. The leading digits 0 and 1 are reserved in the NANP: 0 reaches an operator and 1 is the long-distance trunk prefix, so every area code starts with a digit from 2 through 9.
Is the exchange code the same as the area code?
No. The area code (NPA) covers a region; the exchange code (NXX) identifies one central office inside that region. Both are three digits, but they play different roles.
Why do some newer area codes have a 2, 3 or 4 in the middle?
Because the original format allowed only 0 or 1 there. When that space ran out, the plan was widened to any middle digit, so new codes such as 234 and 332 look unusual next to older ones like 212.
Does an area code show where a phone is right now?
Not reliably. The code reflects where the number was first issued. Number portability and internet telephony mean it can be answered somewhere else entirely.
Are all North American numbers ten digits?
Yes. Every number is three digits of area code, three of exchange code and four of line number. The extra 1 in front of a long-distance number is a dialing prefix, not part of the number itself.
rel: Look up a number or place

title: Overlays vs Splits: Why a City Has Four Area Codes
desc: An overlay adds a new area code over existing territory; a split carves the region in two. How each relief method works and why dialing changes.
h1: Overlay or split: how new area codes arrive
lede: When an area code runs out of numbers, regulators either layer a second code over the same territory or divide the territory in two.
body:
Why area codes run out

An area code holds roughly eight hundred exchange codes, and each exchange code holds ten thousand line numbers. That sounds like millions of numbers, but blocks of ten thousand are handed to carriers in every exchange and much of the capacity sits unused in small towns. As a region adds mobile lines, second lines, alarm circuits and business trunks, the code fills up. When the last exchange code is assigned, regulators must add capacity, and there are only two ways to do it: an overlay or a split.

Overlays: a second code over the same ground

An overlay adds a new area code covering exactly the same territory as the existing one. Nobody's number changes. The old code keeps issuing numbers for as long as it has any, and the new code is used for new lines. Manhattan, for example, is served by 212 together with the overlays 646, 332 and 917. Toronto has 416, 647 and 437 covering the same city. Because two numbers in the same neighbourhood can now begin with different area codes, seven-digit dialing becomes ambiguous, so the whole overlay region moves to ten-digit dialing.

Splits: cutting the territory in two

A split divides the existing area into two geographic pieces. One piece keeps the original code; the other receives a new one, and every number in that piece is renumbered. Miami's 305 was split when Broward County received 954, and Palm Beach later took 561. Splits are disruptive: businesses reprint stationery, signs and advertising, customers relearn numbers, and the change collides with number portability, which was designed to let people keep their numbers. A permissive period usually lets callers use both the old and new codes for a while, but after that the old numbers fail.

Why a city ends up with four codes

Overlays stack. A growing city can pick up a second, third and fourth code over the same footprint, and each addition keeps the earlier ones in service. New York's codes include 212, 332, 646 and 917, plus 718, 347 and 929 for the outer boroughs. None of those codes marks a different neighbourhood; they are the same territory, layered over time. Two numbers with different area codes can sit on the same block.

Who decides

Numbering relief is planned long before exhaustion. The North American Numbering Plan Administrator forecasts when each area code will run out and proposes a relief method, then the public regulator for that country or territory approves it. That lead time is why a new code appears years after it is announced, and why the choice between overlay and split is a regulatory decision rather than a technical necessity.

What it means for you

  • In an overlay area, always dial the area code, even for a local call.
  • Do not assume an unfamiliar area code is far away; overlays sit inside one city.
  • When you order a new line, the carrier may assign either the old code or the new one.
  • Splits are now rare; overlays have been the standard relief method for decades.
faq: Will I have to change my number when an overlay is added?
No. An overlay adds a new code for new numbers only; existing numbers keep the code they already have.
What happens to numbers in a split?
The half of the territory that receives the new code is renumbered into it. Callers usually get a permissive period during which both the old and the new forms work.
Why do regulators prefer overlays?
Overlays avoid forcing customers to change numbers. Splits require renumbering, cost money on both sides and clash with number portability.
Does an overlay change where a number rings?
No. Every code in the overlay covers the same footprint. The difference is administrative, not geographic.
Can I tell an overlay code from an original one?
Not reliably. The original codes tend to be the oldest, but carriers issue numbers in whichever code still has capacity.

title: How to Call the US From Abroad: +1 and Exit Codes
desc: The exact dialing pattern for a US number from another country: the exit code, country code 1, ten digits, and why the leading 1 is dropped.
h1: Calling a United States number from another country
lede: From outside North America the pattern is exit code, then 1, then ten digits, and the leading 1 from the domestic format disappears.
body:
The dialing pattern

From most of the world, a United States number is reached with three pieces: the international access code of the country you are calling from, the country code 1, and the ten digits of the number. Written out, that is exit code + 1 + NPA + NXX + XXXX. A customer in London dialing a New York number types 00 1 212 555 0142. A caller in Berlin types 00 1 415 555 0142. On a mobile phone the plus sign replaces the exit code, so the same number is stored as +1 212 555 0142.

Exit codes differ by country

The exit code, also called the international prefix, belongs to the country you are physically dialing from, not to the number you are calling. Most of Europe, much of Asia and Latin America use 00, sometimes followed by a carrier-selection code. The United States and Canada use 011. Australia uses 0011, Japan uses 010, and South Korea has several competing prefixes. Hotels and office systems often require a digit first to get an outside line, so a caller in a hotel may need to dial 9 before the exit code. Getting this step wrong is the most common reason an international call never leaves the building.

The number one is the country code

The 1 in +1 is not the long-distance 1 you dial at home. It is the country code of the North American Numbering Plan, shared by the United States, Canada and around twenty Caribbean countries and territories, Puerto Rico among them. Because it is a country code, it sits in the same position as 44 for the United Kingdom or 91 for India.

Drop the leading 1

Inside the United States, long-distance numbers are written as 1-212-555-0142. That first 1 is a trunk prefix: it tells the domestic network that a long-distance number follows. When you dial from abroad, the exit code already signals an international call, so the trunk 1 must be dropped. You dial exactly one 1 in total. Dialing 00 1 1 212 inserts a stray digit and the call cannot connect. The same rule applies in reverse: someone in London calling the United States drops the leading 1 from the American number, just as an American calling London drops the leading 0 from 020 7946 0958 and dials 00 44 20 7946 0958.

Common mistakes

  • Dialing the domestic 1 twice: 011 1 1 415 555 0142.
  • Using your home country's exit code while you are travelling in another country.
  • Keeping a trunk zero before a foreign number, as if it were a local prefix.
  • Omitting the country code and dialing ten digits, which works only inside North America.
  • Storing numbers without the plus sign, then trying to call them from a foreign SIM card.

What will not work from abroad

Short codes are local by design. 911, 411, 511 and 988 reach services in the numbering plan you are standing in, not the one you are calling. Toll-free 800 numbers are also awkward: some are reachable from abroad through a special access number, many are not, and any call that does connect may be billed to you.

Before you dial

Check three things: the country code is 1, the next ten digits are the area code plus the number, and the number does not begin with 1. If the number you were given starts with 1, that 1 is the trunk prefix and is dropped from abroad.
faq: Do I dial 011 to call the US from the UK?
No. The UK exit code is 00, so a US number is dialed 00 1 followed by ten digits. The 011 prefix applies when calling from the United States or Canada.
Why does my call fail when I add the 1?
Because the 1 is already there as the country code. Dialing the domestic trunk 1 as well creates an extra digit and the number cannot be completed.
Can I reach a toll-free 800 number from another country?
Sometimes. Many toll-free numbers are reachable from abroad but not all, and the call may be billed, so use the international access number the company publishes.
What does the plus sign in +1 212 555 0142 mean?
It stands for the exit code of the country you are dialing from. Mobile phones translate it automatically; on a landline you type the local exit code instead.
How do I call a mobile phone in the United States?
The same way as a landline: exit code, then 1, then area code and number. US mobile numbers have no special prefix and the caller pays.

title: Ten-Digit Dialing: Why 7-Digit Local Calls Fail
desc: Why you now dial the area code for local calls in the US, what overlays and the 988 short code changed, and what happens if you dial seven digits.
h1: Why you have to dial ten digits now
lede: A local call used to be seven digits; across the North American plan the area code is now part of every number you dial.
body:
What ten-digit dialing means

Ten-digit dialing means typing the area code as part of every local number: NPA + NXX + XXXX. Seven-digit dialing assumed that the caller and the number were in the same area code, so the area code could be left out. That assumption only works while an area has exactly one code. Once a second code covers the same territory, the exchange code alone no longer identifies a unique number, and the area code has to be dialed.

Two forces behind the change

The first is overlays. Metro areas have layered new area codes over old ones for years, and every overlay makes ten-digit dialing mandatory in that region. The second is 988, the three-digit code for the suicide and crisis lifeline. A three-digit code only works if no local seven-digit number can begin with those digits, so in the dozens of area codes where 988 was a valid exchange, seven-digit dialing had to end. Together the two changes have made ten digits the normal way to dial a number across the North American Numbering Plan.

What happens if you dial seven digits

In a ten-digit area, the switch cannot complete the call and plays a recorded announcement asking you to dial the area code. The call does not go to a wrong number; it simply fails. In a single-code area where seven-digit dialing is still permitted, a seven-digit call usually completes, but dialing ten digits also works, so there is no reason to rely on the shorter form.

Does a local call need the leading 1?

No. Ten digits is the whole local number: area code, exchange and line. The 1 remains the long-distance trunk prefix and appears in front of the area code when you call outside your local calling area, as in 1-212-555-0142. Many networks accept ten digits for both local and long-distance calls, and cell phones generally send ten digits regardless of how the number is entered.

Why cell phone users never notice

Contacts are stored with the area code, and the handset always sends the full ten digits, so a mobile caller has effectively dialed ten digits for years. The change bites office phone systems, alarm panels, fax machines and older landlines, which may have been programmed with seven-digit numbers. Reprogramming speed dials and checking the dial plan on a private phone system fixes most complaints.

It is not only the United States

Canada has required ten-digit dialing in overlay regions for a long time, and the same logic applies in any NANP country that adds a code over an existing one. The rule is not about a particular regulator; it is about making every dialed number unambiguous.

How to avoid the recording

  • Save every number with its area code, even local ones.
  • Update speed dials, alarm systems and call lists that still hold seven digits.
  • For long distance, remember the pattern 1 + ten digits.
  • If a call fails, check the area code before assuming the line is dead.
faq: Can I still dial seven digits anywhere?
In a few single-code areas, yes, but the practice is dying out. Ten digits is accepted everywhere in the NANP, so use it.
Did 988 cause ten-digit dialing?
Partly. Overlays had already required it in most metro areas; the 988 rollout forced it in the area codes where a local number could begin with 988.
Do I need a 1 before a local call?
No. A local call is ten digits. The leading 1 is the trunk prefix used for long-distance calls.
Does ten-digit dialing change my phone number?
No. It changes only the number of digits you dial, not the number itself.
How do I fix a phone system that still dials seven digits?
Reprogram the stored numbers with the area code, and check the PBX or key system's dial plan so it accepts ten digits.

title: N11 Codes and Toll-Free Prefixes Explained
desc: What 911, 411, 511, 811, 311 and 988 reach, how N11 short codes are reserved, and how the toll-free prefixes 800 through 888 work.
lede: Short three-digit codes reach services rather than people, and the 8xx prefixes are area codes that bill the receiver instead of the caller.
body:
How N11 codes work

An N11 code is three digits: any first digit from 2 to 9 followed by 1 and 1. The North American Numbering Plan keeps these combinations out of the pool used for area codes and exchange codes, which is exactly why no area code is 911 and no exchange is 411. They are dialed without an area code because they are services, not telephone lines.

What each code reaches

CodeServiceNotes
211Community and social servicesReferral to local health and social programmes; availability varies.
311City government servicesNon-emergency municipal requests; not every city operates it.
411Directory assistanceMay carry a charge, depending on the carrier and plan.
511Traffic and road conditionsOperated by states and provinces; coverage varies.
611Telephone company serviceReaches your own carrier for repairs and account help.
711Telecommunications relayConnects deaf, hard-of-hearing and speech-disabled callers.
811Utility locatingCall before digging; the service notifies buried-line operators.
911EmergencyPolice, fire and ambulance; works across the NANP.

988 is not an N11 code

988, the suicide and crisis lifeline, is a three-digit code but not an N11 code: its last two digits are 88, not 11. It behaves like one in practice, since it is dialed without an area code and works across the United States and Canada. When 988 was introduced, area codes where a local number could begin with those digits had to move to ten-digit dialing so the short code would always be reachable.

Toll-free prefixes are area codes

Toll-free numbers use their own area codes, but the number is otherwise a normal ten-digit NANP number: 1-800-555-0142. The seven toll-free prefixes in service are 800, 833, 844, 855, 866, 877 and 888. Only those seven are used for toll-free service; every other 8xx code is either a geographic area code such as 801 or 808, or is unassigned. The prefix says nothing about where the business is or what kind of line answers. Toll-free numbers are portable and can be routed to any call centre, so an 866 number can be answered in another country.

Who pays

The distinction that matters is billing. A toll-free call is billed to the number's subscriber, not to the caller, which is why 800 numbers are used for sales and support lines. Premium-rate 900 numbers work the other way: the caller is billed, usually a per-minute charge. Some shorter services, such as directory assistance, can also carry a fee that appears on the caller's bill.

Practical limits

  • N11 codes are local: they reach services in the numbering plan you are dialing from.
  • Availability varies; 911 is universal, most others are not guaranteed in every town.
  • Office phone systems sometimes block N11 calls, so a failure may be the PBX, not the network.
  • Toll-free numbers may not be reachable from outside the NANP.
faq: Is 988 an N11 code?
No. N11 codes end in 11; 988 ends in 88. It still works like a short code, dialed without an area code and available nationwide.
Why can't 911 be an area code?
The N11 combinations are reserved for short codes, so they are excluded from area code and exchange code assignment.
Are toll-free numbers free for the caller?
Yes. The subscriber pays for the call and the caller is not charged. A 900 number is the opposite: the caller pays.
Do all N11 services work everywhere?
No. 911 is universal across the NANP, but 211, 311, 511, 711 and 811 are run by local authorities and coverage differs.
Can I call an 800 number from abroad?
Often but not always. Many toll-free numbers can be reached from outside the NANP, some cannot, and the call may be billed to you.

title: Canadian Area Codes: Provinces, Overlays and +1
desc: Canada uses the same +1 numbering plan as the US. How its area codes map to provinces, why overlays are routine, and how calling works.
h1: Canada's area codes, province by province
lede: Canada is a full member of the North American Numbering Plan, so its numbers look American even though Canadian regulators manage the codes.
body:
One numbering plan, two countries

Canada has been part of the North American Numbering Plan from the start, so Canadian numbers use the same ten digits, the same plus-one country code and the same area-code structure as numbers in the United States. A Canadian number is not a US number, however: it is an international call for billing purposes even though the dialing looks identical. From Canada you dial 1 + area code + number for long distance, and from the United States to Canada you dial the same eleven digits.

Who assigns the codes

Canadian numbering is managed separately from the American system. The CRTC sets the rules and the Canadian Numbering Administrator allocates area codes and exchange codes inside Canada. Canadian codes are mixed into the same number space as US ones, with no separate prefix range, which is why Ontario's 613 sits next to US codes such as 612 and 614.

Codes by province

Province or regionArea codes
Ontario, Toronto416, 647, 437
Ontario, Hamilton, Niagara and the GTA905, 289, 365
Ontario, Ottawa and the east613, 343
Ontario, southwest519, 226
Ontario, northeast705, 249
Ontario, northwest807
Quebec, Montreal514, 438
Quebec, around Montreal450, 579
Quebec, Quebec City and the east418, 581
Quebec, Gatineau, Sherbrooke and the west819, 873
British Columbia604, 778, 236 in Vancouver; 250 for the rest of the province
Alberta403, 587, 825 in the south; 780, 587, 825 in the north
Saskatchewan306, 639
Manitoba204, 431
Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island902, 782
New Brunswick506
Newfoundland and Labrador709
Yukon, Northwest Territories and Nunavut867

Codes are added and rearranged as regions grow, so read the table as the long-standing picture rather than a permanent one.

Overlays are routine

Most Canadian population centres have more than one code. Toronto's 416, 647 and 437 cover the same city; Montreal's 514 and 438 do the same; Calgary and Edmonton share the 403, 587 and 825 group in the south and 780, 587 and 825 in the north. As in the United States, an overlay code is not a different neighbourhood, so ten-digit dialing is required across the entire overlay region. New numbers may be issued in any of the codes covering the address.

Why Canada shares +1

The numbering plan was built as one continental system for the telephone network that spanned both countries, and Canada has stayed a full participant while regulating its own portion. That shared root is why a Toronto number looks exactly like a New York number, and why a caller dialing internationally cannot tell the two apart until the area code is checked.

Dialing and billing across the border

Dialing is seamless: 1 + ten digits in both directions, or +1 + ten digits from outside North America. Billing is not. Calls between the two countries are international calls under most plans, so a domestic US minute may not cover a call to Canada. Canadian mobile numbers are billed to the caller, as in the United States.
faq: Is a Canadian number a +1 number?
It is. Canada is a full member of the NANP, so Canadian numbers use country code 1 and ten digits, exactly like US numbers.
Why does Toronto have three area codes?
416 is the original code and 647 and 437 are overlays covering the same city. They do not mark different neighbourhoods.
Do I need to dial 1 to call within Canada?
For long distance, yes: 1 + area code + number. Local calls in overlay areas need ten digits.
Are calls from the US to Canada international?
For billing, usually yes. The dialing format matches a domestic US call, but most plans treat Canada as an international destination.
What is area code 867?
It is the area code for Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut, shared across the three territories.

title: Caribbean Area Codes: Which Islands Use +1
desc: Jamaica, Trinidad, Barbados and more than a dozen other Caribbean places share +1 with the US. Their codes, and why they are still international calls.
h1: Caribbean countries inside the +1 numbering plan
lede: More than a dozen Caribbean countries and territories have North American area codes, but dialing them is usually not a domestic call.
body:
Why Caribbean countries use +1

Over the decades the North American Numbering Plan's Caribbean membership grew, with each country receiving a three-digit code from the same pool used by US states and Canadian provinces. Each is a full NANP member today. That is why a Jamaican number and a New Jersey number have the same shape: country code 1, area code, three-digit exchange, four-digit line. The region once shared a single code, 809; as demand grew each country received its own, and 809 now serves the Dominican Republic alongside 829 and 849.

Which places have +1

Country or territoryArea code
Anguilla264
Antigua and Barbuda268
Bahamas242
Barbados246
Bermuda441
British Virgin Islands284
Cayman Islands345
Dominica767
Dominican Republic809, 829, 849
Grenada473
Jamaica876, 658
Montserrat664
Puerto Rico787, 939
Saint Kitts and Nevis869
Saint Lucia758
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines784
Sint Maarten, Dutch side721
Trinidad and Tobago868
Turks and Caicos Islands649
US Virgin Islands340

Same shape, different billing

Inside the NANP these numbers are dialed with a leading 1 and ten digits, exactly like a domestic US call: 1-876-555-0142 reaches Jamaica. The similarity ends there. For most US carriers a call to a foreign NANP country is an international call: it may be billed per minute, it may be excluded from domestic calling plans, and it may not be covered by an international add-on. Your phone will happily dial it without warning.

Not US domestic calls

Two exceptions deserve care. Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands are US territories, and most US carriers treat calls to them as domestic. Elsewhere in the region, from Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago to Barbados and the Cayman Islands, treat the call as international unless your plan explicitly says otherwise. Prepaid balances can drain quickly at international rates.

From outside the NANP

The format is exit code + 1 + area code + number, the same as calling the United States or Canada. Someone in Britain calling Jamaica dials 00 1 876 555 0142. The country code is still 1, because the Caribbean countries are NANP members; there is no separate country code for each island.

Places that are not on +1

Not every Caribbean destination belongs to the plan. Haiti uses 509, Cuba uses 53, Aruba uses 297, Curacao and Bonaire use 599, Guadeloupe uses 590 and Martinique uses 596. If the number you are calling does not start with +1, the pattern above does not apply.

Why the code does not pin the island

Area codes do not always identify one place on a map. The Dominican Republic has three codes over one territory, Jamaica has two, and internet telephony means a number can be answered far from where it was issued. Use the area code as a strong clue, then confirm the destination before you send anything important.
faq: Is calling Jamaica from the US an international call?
Yes. Jamaica is a NANP member, so you dial 1 plus ten digits, but most US carriers bill the call as international.
Which Caribbean numbers are included in US domestic plans?
Generally Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands, because they are US territories. Other islands are usually international; check your plan.
Do I need a different country code for each island?
No. They share country code 1, the same as the US and Canada. The area code identifies the country or territory.
Which Caribbean destinations are not on +1?
Haiti uses 509, Cuba 53, Aruba 297, Curacao and Bonaire 599, Guadeloupe 590 and Martinique 596, among others.
Does 911 work in the Caribbean?
Emergency numbers are set nationally and vary by country. 911 is common in the region but not guaranteed, so check the local emergency number.

title: How to Find Your Area Code: Lookups and Rate Centres
desc: Find the area code for an address or ZIP the reliable way: rate centres, overlays, portability, and why a number's code may not match its location.
h1: Finding the right area code for an address
lede: The area code for an address follows the telephone exchange that serves it, not the city name or the ZIP code alone.
body:
Start with what you are trying to find

People search for an area code for two very different reasons. One is identifying a number they already have: the first three digits are the area code, and the question is what region it belongs to. The other is obtaining a number for an address, for a new line, a new office or a VoIP account. The first is a decoding problem, the second is a coverage problem, and they need different lookups.

An area code is tied to an exchange, not a ZIP code

Central office codes are assigned to rate centres, and a rate centre is the town or exchange area a call is rated and priced against. A ZIP code can straddle two or three rate centres, and a city can be carved into several of them, so a ZIP lookup can return more than one plausible area code. Border areas make it harder: houses on the same street can sit in different exchanges and even different states. If accuracy matters, look up the exchange, not the postcode.

What a rate centre is

A rate centre is a geographic unit used for telephone pricing. It defines which calls count as local, which are toll, and how a central office code is grouped for billing. Each NXX belongs to exactly one rate centre, but one rate centre can hold many NXX codes and, in an overlay region, more than one area code. Rate centres are the reason a large city can be split into dozens of exchanges while a small town shares one exchange with its neighbours.

Reading an existing number

Split the number: NPA is the first three digits, NXX is the next three, and the last four are the line. Look up the NPA for the general region, then the NXX to narrow it to the exchange that serves a specific town. Directories and carrier databases do this together, which is why a lookup that returns only an area code can be less useful than one that returns the exchange and its town.

Caveats that change the answer

  • Number portability: a ported number keeps its original area code even after the customer moves or changes carrier.
  • VoIP and cloud telephony: providers issue numbers for markets they serve, so a business can hold a number from another state.
  • Overlays: a single address may have several valid codes, and none is more correct than the others.
  • New development: a new estate may be served by one exchange even though neighbouring streets use another.
  • Old maps: area code maps in marketing material are often out of date, and boundary lines are approximate.

Getting a number for an address

Ask the carrier what area codes it can assign at that address. In overlay markets the answer is usually several codes for one location, and the carrier may let you choose. If you are moving an existing number, porting keeps the old code, which is why people who move across the country often keep a number that does not match their new home.

Confirming before you rely on it

Use two sources when the answer matters: a directory like this one for the region and exchange, and the carrier for the specific line. A number that looks wrong is usually ported, on a VoIP plan, or in an overlay region rather than misprinted.
faq: Can I find an area code from a ZIP code?
Only approximately. ZIPs can span several rate centres, and overlay regions have more than one area code, so a ZIP narrows the search but does not settle it.
What is a rate centre?
The exchange area a telephone number is rated against. Each exchange code belongs to one, and rate centres decide which calls count as local.
Why does a number's area code not match where the person lives?
Number portability and VoIP. A number keeps the code it was issued with, wherever the customer later moves or whichever provider answers it.
Can I choose my area code?
Sometimes. In overlay regions the carrier may offer several codes for the same address; otherwise it assigns what the exchange has available.
How do I verify an area code before relying on it?
Check the exchange code against a directory and confirm with the carrier. Two sources catch porting and overlay confusion.
